documents.title: Anorectal malformation and outcome review (ARMOUR) project: a systematic review for the outcomes reported in patients with an anorectal malformation.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Being born with an anorectal malformation (ARM) often leads to lifelong issues with faecal and urinary function, as well as challenges in sexual, emotional and psychosocial development. Even when anatomical correction is achieved, full functional recovery is not guaranteed. Despite several international consensus meetings with leading medical professionals in the ARM field, there is still no agreement on the essential outcome domains that should be measured for ARM treatment and follow-up. Therefore, the goal of this systematic review is to identify all the outcomes reported in literature.
METHODS: This systematic review adhered to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, aiming to identify all short- and long-term outcomes in ARM studies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase for studies from 1 January 2009 to 1 May 2023, using terms related to 'anorectal malformation'. The Cochrane Library was also searched, but no relevant reviews were found. Eligibility criteria included studies mentioning ARM outcomes in the title or abstract. Exclusions were non-mention of ARM outcomes, lack of full text, and non-English or non-Dutch language. Data extraction by two reviewers captured author details, study design, patient characteristics, ARM types and outcomes, categorised by occurrence time and reporter. Outcomes were consolidated from 339 unique outcomes into 25 domains according to the Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trial () taxonomy and categorised into five core areas: 'mortality/survival', 'physiological/clinical', 'life impact', 'resource use' and 'adverse events'.
RESULTS: Out of 348 eligible studies, 118 met the inclusion criteria. These were mostly conducted in Europe (47%), Asia (34%) and North America (11%), with designs including retrospective (36%), cross-sectional (23%) and case reports/series (18%). Patient numbers ranged from 1 to 1206, with many studies lacking clear descriptions of surgical techniques (29%) and age categories (21%). A total of 339 outcomes were identified, categorised into 25 domains per the COMET taxonomy. Mentioned most frequently were 'physiological/clinical' outcomes (772 mentions), with 'gastrointestinal outcomes' being predominant. Long-term outcomes were most common (71%), followed by both short and long term (16%), and short term (13%). Outcomes were mainly reported by medical professionals (59%), with only 10% being patient-reported outcomes. Various measurement tools were used, including validated and self-made instruments, with the international classification (Krickenbeck) being the most used rating scale for postoperative results. Many studies lacked detailed descriptions and validation of their measurement methods.The identified outcomes in this review will be used as an input to eventually develop a Core Outcome Set.

In the literature, short- and long-term outcomes are reported inconsistently and selectively due to significant differences in how they are documented. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study shows a high variability in outcomes reporting, where many different measurement instruments were being used. There is no standardisation in outcome measuring and reporting. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This systematic review is a part of the anorectal malformation and outcome review project where the aim is to develop a Core Outcome Set after identifying and categorising all the reported outcomes in this study. Introduction An anorectal malformation (ARM) is a relatively rare congenital malformation in which the anus and rectum have not been developed properly. The incidence is 1 to 5000 live births. 1 6 Although surgical repair is a requirement, it certainly does not necessarily resolve all challenges in the long term. For a long time, treatment was considered complete after surgery. However, nowadays, there is increasing attention to long-term problems, and follow-up care has become more common. This particularly focuses on faecal and urinary incontinence. Additionally, an ARM is part of the vertebral defect, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, renal anomalies and limbs anomalies (VACTERL) association, which also deserves attention during follow-up. Faecal and urinary incontinence and/or obstipation are well known problems in adolescence and adulthood, 7 8 but the challenges faced by patients with an ARM have proven to be much broader than previously thought, with issues such as sexual dysfunction and psychological well-being, to name a few, being equally important. 9 15 Lately, physicians are acknowledging that these daily encountered problems are very significant to patients. Even though there are standardised treatments for patients with ARM, there is still no standardised follow-up protocol that ensures consistent and comprehensive reporting of outcomes, nor a long-term care pathway that addresses the broader needs of patients. Consequently, the clinical value of these outcome measures remains unclear, and it is uncertain whether patients find them significant. This lack of clarity complicates the comparison between studies and highlights the absence of a structured follow-up for individual patients. The primary goal of the ARM and outcome review (ARMOUR) project is to develop a Core Outcome Set (COS), representing the minimum set of outcomes reported by patients and healthcare professionals involved in ARM treatment, that can be implemented in an effective care pathway to support individual ARM management decisions. This systematic review, as a part of the ARMOUR-project, aims to identify candidate outcomes related to ARM available in academic literature. Materials and methods Study design This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) statement and a checklist and flowchart were used in order to achieve the highest standard in reporting items for this systematic review. The ARMOUR study has been registered in the Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) database on 26 September 2019 ( https://www.comet-initiative.org/Studies/Details/1413 ). Search strategy A systematic literature search was conducted using both PubMed and Embase databases, in order to identify all studies describing important outcomes regarding all types of ARM between the first of January 2009 and the first of May 2023. The search showed that over 80% of articles were published in this period, and including earlier years would have added more articles but not more outcomes. The Cochrane Library for Systematic Reviews was also searched for results regarding outcomes in ARM, but between 01/01/2009 and 05/01/2023, there were no reviews available. The search terms were drafted with the help of an information specialist using search terms relating to ‘anorectal malformation’. There were no restrictions related to study type. The search was narrowed down to studies concerning humans. The main research terms were used were: “Anorectal Malformations”[Mesh] OR “Anus, Imperforate”[Mesh] OR Atresia ani[tiab] OR ((“Anal Canal”[Mesh] OR Canalis analis[tiab] OR Anus (tiab) OR Anal [tiab] OR Rectal [tiab] OR Anorectal [tiab]) AND (Malformation* [tiab] OR Anomal*[tiab] OR Atresia* [tiab] OR Agenes* [tiab] OR Imperforat* [tiab] OR Stenos* [tiab])) NOT ((“Animals”[Mesh]) NOT “Humans”[Mesh]) AND (“2009/01/01”[PDAT] : “2023/05/01”[PDAT]). For more details, see online supplemental appendix A . Eligibility criteria The titles and abstracts of all papers regarding ARM identified through the literature search were reviewed and assessed for suitability and relevance by a team of two independent reviewers (CR/SC and SC/LH). Disagreements were resolved by a fourth reviewer (RV). The opinion of the fourth reviewer was regarded as decisive for inclusion of a study. Papers that were considered eligible for inclusion were any studies that mentioned outcome(s) regarding ARM in the title or abstract of the paper. To ensure the broadest possible collection of evidence for evaluation, all study types were included in the review. Papers were excluded if there was no mentioning of ARM and outcomes related to them, had no full text available, or were not written in English or Dutch. Data extraction and quality assessment Data extraction was conducted independently by a team of two reviewers (CR/SC and SC/LH) using a predefined data collection form in Microsoft Excel designed to capture the relevant information from the papers. The collected data included the name of the authors, year of publication, study design, baseline characteristics of the included patient population, the number of patients, characteristics of the type of ARM, in- and exclusion criteria and all data related to defined outcomes concerning ARM. Data discrepancies were discussed, with the final decision made by the fourth reviewer (RV). Outcomes were categorised as being short term if they emerged within the first year after birth, long term if they emerged after the first year of life or both. Also, it was noted by whom the outcomes mentioned in a study were reported: clinical records/medical professionals (only), patients, parents/caregivers (only), patients and their parents/caregivers (only) or all groups. The quality of the studies included in our systematic review was not determined, because the aim of the systematic review was to include all reported outcomes concerning patients with ARM. Therefore, also case reports, uncontrolled trials and observational studies were included, as long as all reported outcomes in literature were covered. Hence, no risk of bias assessment was performed. The list of extracted outcomes was shortened by merging similar outcomes to create a clear overview, for example, ‘dietary changes’ contained ‘dietary therapy’, ‘dietary measures’, and ‘dietary modification’. This process resulted in 339 different outcomes. These 339 outcomes were then classified into 25 outcome domains according to the COMET taxonomy with the number of studies and percentage of studies that report a specific outcome and whether an outcome was reported by medical professionals, patients or parents/caregivers ( online supplemental appendix B ). The domains were classified into five core areas: ‘mortality/survival’, ‘physiological/clinical’, ‘life impact’, ‘resource use’ and ‘adverse events’ ( figure 1 ). For the domain with the highest number of reported outcomes, we applied our own domain categorisation to maintain a clear overview. Figure 1 Core areas and domains. Patient and public involvement There was no patient involvement for this systematic review. Results Search and selection of studies After removal of duplicates, 348 full-text studies were found. Of these, 118 studies met the predefined inclusion criteria, including ten studies extracted from systematic reviews ( figure 2 ). The used literature search for PubMed and EMBASE is presented in online supplemental appendix A . In online supplemental appendix C , all included studies are listed, while table 1 shows some of the characteristics of these studies. Details of data extraction are retrievable via the author. Figure 2 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) flow diagram showing identification, screening, eligibility and inclusion of studies on outcomes of patients born with anorectal malformation who underwent operative treatment. Study characteristics The majority of studies was conducted in Europe (47%), followed by Asia (34%) and North America (11%). Three studies were conducted in Africa; four studies were executed elsewhere. Twenty-seven percent of all included studies even compared between several techniques or described more than one. Also, some studies described additional non-surgical interventions such as dilatations, various bowel management programmes or transanal irrigations. However, in 29% of the studies, no clear description of the investigated surgical technique could be found. Most studies had a retrospective design (36%), followed by cross-sectional studies (23%) and case reports or case series (18%). The number of patients included per study ranged from 1 to 1206 ARM patients. However, most samples were of relatively small to medium magnitude (ie, between five and 70 Patients). In 12% of the studies, the age of the study population was unknown, or the age category was not described clearly. If the age was described, it mostly concerned the age category 0–17 years old (58% of the studies), followed by research on patient samples consisting of children as well as adults (22%). If applicable, other anomalies co-occurring with ARM were described, such as urogenital defects, sacral anomalies and neurological problems. Most studies explicitly mentioned, when applicable, the presence of a diagnosed syndrome in patients such as VACTERL or other clusters of congenital defects alongside the ARM. In 8% of the studies, there was no mentioning of the type of ARM that was investigated. In all other studies, at least the ARM was categorised as high, intermediate and low, as proposed in 1970. 16 17 Most studies (40%) used the most recent international acknowledged and standardised Krickenbeck classification system, published in 2005, to describe the type of ARM according to the type of fistula. 18 Some studies only included one type of fistula, others described more than one type and/or included patients with complex anomalies. Identification of outcomes A large variety of outcomes was reported in the 118 included studies, showing considerable heterogeneity among studies, even among studies reviewing the same surgical technique. In many articles, no clear definitions of the outcomes were provided. Most studies reported outcomes that were long-term outcomes (71%); after that, the most outcomes reported were both short and long term (16%), followed by short-term outcomes (13%). Outcome domain All the reported outcomes are categorised into 25 domains, which fall under five core areas ( figure 1 ). Outcomes in the core area ‘physiological/clinical’ were reported 772 times in the included studies. Within this core area, ‘gastrointestinal outcomes’ was the most frequently reported domain comprising 110 different outcomes, and ‘constipation’ as the most frequently reported outcome among these (57 studies, 48%). These 110 outcomes were therefore subdivided into five different domains during extraction, for the purpose of creating a clear overview. The outcomes were arranged as ‘postoperative complications’, ‘pre- and perioperative complications’, ‘bowel function’, ‘anorectal manometry evaluation and other measurements’, and ‘stoma problems’, as displayed in figure 3 and more in detail in online supplemental appendix D . Figure 3 Frequency of outcome reporting according to own categorisation. Outcomes concerning the ‘renal and urinary outcomes’ domain were mentioned 155 times, which turned out to be the second-most reported outcome domain. The least mentioned outcome domain was ‘economic recourse use’ where only one outcome was evaluated: ‘costs of hospitalisation’. The domains ‘immune system outcomes’ and ‘vascular outcomes’ were not reported. Also, outcomes regarding pregnancy and perinatal issues were not often reported: the outcome ‘spontaneous pregnancy’ was reported in four studies (3%). Furthermore, outcomes in the domain ‘adverse events’ were only described by studies conducting research on the effectiveness of at least one surgical technique or a comparison between two techniques. ‘Blood loss’ was the most frequently assessed outcome in the domain ‘adverse events’ (six studies, 5%). No mortality was reported in the six studies (5%) that covered the core area of ‘mortality/survival’. 70 (59%) studies measured outcomes as reported by clinical records/medical professionals, followed by only 24 studies (20%) where the outcomes were mainly reported by patients, with a few additional questions filled out by their medical professionals. For example, these studies often used a questionnaire like the Krickenbeck postoperative results questionnaire, 18 but in addition. patients were asked about their sexual functioning or social relations. Outcome measurement instruments A wide range (99) of modalities or tools were used to measure the outcomes, varying from widely known and validated instruments like radiological imaging, urodynamic studies, histology, laboratory analysis and patient-reported outcome measurement instruments (PROMs) (Rintala score, Bowel Function score and the Zarit Burden score), as well as self-made measurement instruments, including questionnaires; rating scales; and open-ended questions in semistructured interviews conducted in patients, parents or teachers. But for many outcomes, details on how they were measured were missing. Some articles described that the used (patient-reported) outcome measures were tested for reliability and validity in patients with ARM but many studies that used a self-made outcome measurement instrument did not. For the ‘physiological/clinical–general’ outcomes, diagnostic tools (including MRI, X-ray, urodynamic studies or voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG)) were mainly used. The most described rating scale in the core area ‘physiological/clinical’ was the international classification (Krickenbeck 18 ) of postoperative results, followed by the Japanese Study Group of Anorectal Anomalies (JSGA) scoring system 19 and the Kelly score. 20 These rating scales, listed as ‘physiological/clinical – satisfaction (aesthetic or functional) after treatment’, are predominantly used by medical professionals to assess the functional outcome of a patient after surgical treatment, though some of them, like the JSGA scoring system, 19 were also used as PROMs. ‘Life impact – (disease-specific) quality of life’ outcomes were measured by validated PROMs or by self-made and non-validated questionnaires or they were measured by qualitative research where semistructured individual interviews were used ( online supplemental appendix E ). Discussion This systematic review revealed a wide variety of outcomes measured in ARM management and follow-up research, emphasising the need for a COS to move towards consistent assessment of outcomes for clinical follow-up. We subdivided five core areas into 25 outcome domains, organising the 339 different outcomes within them and identified 99 measurement modalities or instruments across 118 ARM studies, highlighting significant variation in measures used for the same outcomes within all core areas. This variability severely hampers evidence synthesis. The use of a standardised COS, where outcomes are measured and classified in the same way, is crucial for comparing patient populations, their treatments, and reported outcomes. This is essential for improving patient care and tailoring follow-up strategies effectively to address the diverse needs of patients. Despite the expected heterogeneity due to the inclusion of studies with diverse surgical techniques, co-interventions and objectives, we found substantial heterogeneity even among studies evaluating similar surgical techniques or patient populations. This was exacerbated by the absence of standardised outcome definitions, leading to uncertainty in interpretation. Furthermore, in the same outcome may be assessed by different measurement instruments, further hampering evidence synthesis. Many studies fail to specify the measurement instruments they used. The frequent reporting of outcomes like ‘voluntary bowel movements,’ ‘soiling’ and ‘constipation’ may result from the use of standardised classifications such as the International Classification (Krickenbeck), 18 the JSGA score, 19 the Kelly score 20 or the Rintala score of continence. 1 Consistent follow-up assessments and comprehensive reporting are vital to understanding and addressing these outcomes effectively. It is important to note that the frequency of reporting an outcome does not necessarily indicate its importance. For instance, ‘rectal mucosal prolapse’ is more frequently reported than ‘quality of life’. The former is typically reported by medical professionals, while the latter may be more important to patients. PROs have gained significance in clinical research, providing valuable insights into quality of life, symptom experiences, treatment effects and overall well-being. Although surgical intervention is the primary treatment for ARM, it does not guarantee complete recovery of anorectal function. Persistent issues such as soiling, incontinence, redo-operations and urinary problems significantly impact patient well-being and are a primary focus of medical research. This review identified a relatively low number of PROs in ARM research. While some questionnaires were suitable for measuring PROs, they were only used in a few studies, resulting in limited representation of patient-based evidence. Additionally, few rating systems or questionnaires were disease-specific or validated for the ARM patient population. This lack of data highlights the challenges in capturing the perspectives and experiences of patients, particularly since the ARM population often includes infants, making it difficult to find appropriate proxy measures. A stronger focus on comprehensive follow-up and broader knowledge of outcomes is essential for enhancing patient care and addressing the diverse needs of the ARM patient population. This systematic review identifies clinical and PROs in ARM patients. In the next step of this project, qualitative interviews with patients and caregivers will be held to ensure outcomes from their perspectives. This will be followed by a Delphi process where medical experts, clinical researchers and patients will prioritise outcomes. A final consensus meeting will establish the COS as an evaluation in a life-long ARM care pathway. By establishing a COS for ARM management and follow-up, our project aims to standardise outcome reporting and enhance the comparability and quality of future research. This approach has already yielded significant benefits in other fields. In rheumatoid arthritis, the OMERACT/ACR Core Set (1994) introduced standardised measures—such as tender and swollen joint counts, patient and physician global assessments, and acute-phase reactants—which led to 60%–70% of RA trials adopting the COS and nearly 90% of trialists expressing willingness to use it in new studies. 21 Similarly, in colorectal cancer surgery, a COS developed through systematic literature reviews, interviews, Delphi surveys and consensus meetings achieved uniform reporting across trials by focusing on domains like survival, surgical complications and quality of life. 22 We anticipate that a COS for ARM will have parallel impact: by aligning outcomes and definitions across clinical and patient-reported domains, it will facilitate robust meta-analyses, guide evidence-based clinical decision-making and ultimately support more patient-centred and effective long-term care pathways. Strengths and limitations This study is, to our knowledge, the first to extract various outcomes reported in the literature concerning ARM, aiming to develop a COS. This effort is crucial for research and the development of a standardised care pathway for ARM patients. One of the primary strengths of creating a COS is the enhanced comparability it will provide. By standardising outcomes, outcome reporting bias can be reduced, ensuring that all relevant outcomes are consistently reported and not selectively chosen based on the results. This will also ensure that the outcomes measured are important to both ARM patients and healthcare providers, thus enhancing the applicability of findings to clinical practice. A significant strength of this study is the identification of a large number of outcomes, but there is a limitation regarding the inclusion of PROs. This gap highlights the need for greater emphasis on integrating patient perspectives into the COS. Also, standardised outcomes may restrict researchers from exploring novel or emerging outcomes that could be important in specific contexts or populations. Another limitation is the potential for inconsistency. If the COS is not universally adopted or implemented inconsistently, its benefits can be significantly undermined. Moreover, an overemphasis on standardisation might overlook individual patient differences and unique aspects of certain patients. Furthermore, this study includes literature from 2009 to 2023, while the preferred technique for the surgical management of ARM was introduced in 1982. Including studies from 1982 onwards was not feasible, necessitating a narrowing of the inclusion criteria. Finally, a COS requires regular updates to remain relevant and incorporate new evidence or evolving patient priorities, presenting a continuous challenge for researchers and stakeholders. Future directions The systematic review is the first step in the development of a COS for ARM management and follow-up in a clinical setting and in research. Next steps include interviews with patients and their parents/caregivers to further identify relevant outcomes, followed by the Delphi rounds with clinical experts and patients to achieve consensus on the minimal, most important outcome set. A final step will be the selection of modalities and instruments to assess the outcomes of the COS. Since this review identified a limited representation of patient perspectives, it is essential that patients are deeply involved in this development process. Additionally, involving patients is crucial to ensure their perspectives are represented throughout the care pathway. Conclusion This systematic review highlights significant variability in outcome reporting and assessment in ARM research, with a broad spectrum of outcomes reported by both patients and clinicians/medical professionals. The outcomes are described and measured differently across studies, making comparisons challenging. There is a lack of consistency in outcome reporting, and the patient’s perspective is not always the primary focus. To improve the quality of evidence, it is crucial to develop a COS to standardise outcomes. Additionally, involving patients is essential to ensure their perspectives are integrated throughout the care process. Objectives This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the benefits and harms of surgical interventions for treating vesicovaginal fistula in women. status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Collection date 2026. Background Description of the condition Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a condition characterised by the formation of abnormal communication between the vagina and the bladder. The most common symptom is continuous leakage of urine through the vagina. The occurrence of VVF is generally associated with childbirth, or after surgery or radiotherapy. The aetiology and incidence of VVF vary geographically with the associated cause, as described below. Aetiology of VVF The most common cause of VVFs is obstructed labour. Over 90% of VVFs that occur in women living in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs) are related to childbirth [ 1 , 2 ]. It has been estimated that at least two million women are living with untreated obstetric fistula, with approximately 50,000 to 100,000 new cases occurring annually, mainly in low‐resource settings [ 3 , 4 ]. However, population‐based estimates restricted to clinically confirmed cases suggest lower point estimates: a 2013 systematic review and meta‐analysis reported a prevalence of 0.29 per 1000 women of reproductive age and an incidence of 0.09 per 1000 among recently pregnant women, with higher prevalence in sub‐Saharan Africa (1.60/1000) and South Asia (1.20/1000). These figures may still be conservative due to data scarcity and heterogeneity [ 5 ]. More recently, a large‐scale national survey empirically estimated that in Bangladesh alone there are about 17,500 women aged 15 to 64 years living with obstetric fistula [ 6 ]. Obstetric VVF due to obstructed labour is also associated with many other comorbidities, collectively known as the obstructed labour injury complex [ 7 ], which form not as ‘point’ lesions but as field damage due to extensive tissue necrosis. In other words, many women with VVF due to obstructed labour can suffer urologic and gynaecologic injuries, primary conditions (such as gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and neurologic injury), and secondary conditions (such as dermatologic, reproductive, and social injury). The anatomical sites of injury can be diverse, including urethral loss, rectovaginal fistula, ureteric obstruction leading to hydroureteronephrosis (a condition in which the renal pelvis/calyces and ureter become dilated due to a complete or partial obstruction in the outflow of urine) and renal failure, faecal incontinence secondary to anal sphincter incompetence, amenorrhoea (the absence of a menstrual period in a female organism who has reached reproductive age), secondary infertility, osteitis pubis (a noninfectious inflammation of the pubic symphysis), and foot drop resulting from peroneal nerve palsy (a paralysis on the common fibular nerve that affects the patient's ability to lift the foot at the ankle) [ 7 ]. These concurrent injuries are just as significant. Although improving the modalities for VVF treatment is essential in LMICs, prevention by providing timely access to obstetric care, which includes access to high‐quality caesarean section and improved surgical training in operative obstetrics, is of primary importance [ 8 ]. Furthermore, the occurrence of VVF is uncommon in high‐income countries (HICs): three‐quarters of the cases in such countries are associated with iatrogenic factors (surgery or radiotherapy) [ 9 ], and many of these are due to gynaecological surgery. In a 2016 review of fistulae managed in HICs, 83.2% followed surgery and 13.0% followed radiotherapy, and hysterectomy accounted for a substantial proportion of surgically related cases [ 1 ]. Iatrogenic VVF is generally considered to result from either inadequate repair of an intraoperative bladder injury or from an unrecognised bladder injury during surgery (including delayed thermal injury). This leads to the formation of a urinoma, followed by urinary leakage through the vaginal cuff, eventually resulting in fistula formation. Therefore, this bladder‐vaginal fistula is sometimes referred to as a vesicovaginal vault fistula [ 10 ]. The rate of VVF in the UK is one in 788 hysterectomies; however, it is higher (one in 87) after radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer [ 11 ]. It is also reported that the number of iatrogenic VVF cases is gradually increasing in LMICs and also in HICs [ 12 ]. Radiation therapy is also an important cause of VVF. It has been reported that approximately 0.6% to 2% of women who undergo radiation therapy for cervical cancer eventually develop VVF [ 13 ], whereas more contemporary, image‐guided adaptive brachytherapy data report an incidence of about 0.7% in women without baseline bladder invasion [ 14 ]; in some cases, the fistula may occur several years after the completion of radiation treatment [ 15 ]. Therefore, when VVF is suspected, it is essential to confirm any history of prior pelvic radiation. The tissue surrounding VVF following radiation therapy often shows ischaemic changes (i.e. a restriction in blood supply to the tissue, causing a shortage of oxygen) and is generally of poor tissue quality. To summarise, obstetric VVF resulting from obstructed labour predominantly occurs in LMICs, typically affecting younger women and arising in the postpartum period. The condition of the fistula is often complicated by ischaemic tissue damage, with extensive loss of surrounding tissues and vaginal fibrosis (i.e. the development of fibrous connective tissue in response to an injury), sometimes involving adjacent structures such as the urethra and rectum. Additionally, the surgical repair environment is frequently suboptimal in these settings. In contrast, iatrogenic VVF is more common in HICs, generally affects older women compared with obstetric VVF, and typically presents with minimal tissue loss. Even when fibrosis is present, it is usually localised around the surgical site and does not involve other parts of the vagina. Furthermore, the conditions for surgical repair are often more favourable than in cases of obstetric VVF. Given these distinct differences in the epidemiological background and pathophysiological mechanisms between obstetric and iatrogenic VVF, they should be considered separately. Additionally, standardisation is important because of the wide variety of fistula conditions in either type of VVF. In this regard, Goh’s classification provides a useful system that includes the size of the fistula, vaginal length, the degree of surrounding fibrosis, and the number of previous repair attempts. Additionally, by using a fixed anatomical reference point (the external urethral meatus) to determine the location of the fistula, this system helps reduce subjective variability in assessment and facilitates comparison between studies [ 16 ]. In addition to impairing the woman’s quality of life (QoL) due to continuous urine leakage, VVFs have also been associated with significant psychological distress [ 17 ]. It has been reported that 97% of women with VVF screened positive for potential mental health problems [ 18 ]. Description of the intervention and how it might work Various conservative or minimally invasive therapies are available for VVFs. However, the true effectiveness and success of these treatment modalities are still unknown. The most conservative treatment for VVF is prolonged bladder drainage with a Foley catheter. According to a large study [ 19 ], early continuous drainage within four to six weeks postpartum may result in spontaneous fistula closure, although the exact correction rate is not certain. In general, a minority of cases can be treated with continuous drainage alone, and this therapy is only effective for small, fresh, and simple fistulas [ 20 ]. In cases where simple techniques are unsuccessful or where the size of the VVF is too large to be treated conservatively, surgical intervention is required. Surgical approaches may be vaginal or abdominal (laparotomy, laparoscopic, and robotic), depending on the type of fistula, the woman's characteristics, and the surgeon's experience. The reported success rate varies from 40% to 100%, although defining success is difficult. In general, post‐repair status is defined separately as ‘fistula closed and patient dry’, ‘fistula closed but patient has persistent transurethral incontinence for some reason’, and ‘failure to close the fistula’ [ 1 , 21 ]. The transvaginal approach is generally preferred and is often used in cases where the fistula can be adequately identified from the vaginal view, and those without concurrent abdominal pathology [ 22 ]. The transvaginal approach involves two main approaches, i.e. excision of the vaginal epithelium and partial colpocleisis, which is a surgical procedure involving imbrication of the surrounding fibromuscular tissue typically in an anterior‐to‐posterior fashion (Latzko procedure) [ 23 ], and a multi‐layered closure. The Latzko procedure is a partial colpocleisis without excision of the fistula tract. In the multi‐layered technique, the vaginal epithelium around the fistula is initially incised. After incision, a sufficient amount of the vaginal epithelium is separated from the underlying fibromuscular layer to allow tension‐free closure of the tissue. Whether to freshen (trim) the fistula edges remains a matter of debate. However, unlike the Latzko procedure, wide mobilisation between the bladder and the vagina is essential. After adequate mobilisation, a layered closure is performed. The bladder can be closed either in a single layer or in two layers (mucosa and muscularis/detrusor). Finally, the remaining vaginal epithelium is closed. Transabdominal surgery can be performed using two main approaches, i.e. transvesical and extravesical. The transvesical approach was described by O'Conor in 1951 [ 24 ], and remains the gold standard treatment. This approach involves a cystotomy and direct closure of the fistula. A cystotomy enables complete visualisation of the fistula tract and both the ureteral orifices. The fistula is excised through the vaginal and bladder walls, and the vaginal wall is sutured separately again. The extravesical approach, as described in the late 1990s [ 25 ], is performed without a cystotomy. This method involves dissection of the surface between the vagina and the bladder without cystotomy, where the fistula is closed. It is therefore considered less invasive, as it minimises bladder loss [ 26 ]. However, both approaches remain controversial, and the approach that is actually implemented is often determined by the surgeon's preference. In recent years, there have been increasing reports of laparoscopic and robot‐assisted procedures for these abdominal approaches in HICs [ 27 ]. The advantages of transvaginal repair include shorter operative time, less blood loss, less postoperative pain, and shorter hospital stay than that of transabdominal repair. Conversely, transabdominal surgery is performed in cases with the following characteristics: ureteric orifices are close to the fistula and need to be re‐implanted; fistula is high and difficult to observe transvaginally; or bladder augmentation is necessary. Generally, after either procedure, urine is drained from the bladder continuously for several weeks using a transurethral Foley catheter. The interposition flap has traditionally been used in both transabdominal and transvaginal repair of VVFs to increase the success rates. The Martius flap (Labia majora fat‐flap) is most commonly used to reinforce repairs in the vaginal vault [ 28 ]. In some cases, the gracilis muscle [ 29 ], gluteal muscle, or peritoneum grafts and flaps [ 30 ], are also sometimes used. In contrast, the omentum, peritoneum, or tinea epiploicae of the sigmoid colon are the most commonly used interposition flaps in transabdominal repair [ 31 ]. These flaps add strength, support, and blood supply and seal the fistula. However, harvesting Martius flaps and gracilis muscle flaps is associated with complications such as seroma, haematoma, numbness, pain, and labial distortion. Further, adding an omentum flap may cause postoperative abdominal pain and temporary ileus. Therefore, the use of interposition flaps to repair VVFs is controversial. Surgical repair closes the fistula and prevents a continual flow of urine from the vagina. Successful repair is dependent upon the condition of the fistula, such as the degree of scarring and associated comorbidities. In terms of the repair process, it depends on sufficient mobility of the fistula, tension‐free closure, locating and reliably protecting the ureter, obtaining watertight closure after repair, and long‐term continuous postoperative bladder drainage [ 22 ]. In addition, interposition flaps are used to strengthen the space between the sutured bladder and anterior vaginal wall. Moreover, the use of an interposition flap may reduce recurrence and dyspareunia (pain during intercourse, often related to postoperative vaginal scarring) [ 32 ]. Furthermore, surgical treatment of VVFs also has psychological benefits [ 33 , 34 ]. However, success should not be judged solely on the basis of ‘fistula closure’, especially with regard to obstetric fistulas. True success is indicated when the repair of the fistula results in normal bladder storage and drainage functions, a return to normal sexual function, and especially when the woman is once again accepted as a participant in the family and also in the surrounding community and neighbourhood. Complications The ureters may be inadvertently ligated (that is, a stitch placed to close the fistula may accidentally catch or close the nearby ureteric opening, blocking urine flow from the kidney), in which case additional surgery will be required. In addition, the use of an interposition flap may cause postoperative sequelae, such as pain and neuropathy. Other complications are the same as those of other types of gynaecological surgery, such as bleeding and infection. Why it is important to do this review Although obstetric VVF is not a major problem in high‐income countries, the condition adversely affects millions of women in LMICs and requires urgent and sustained action [ 35 ]. Improving perinatal care in LMICs, by providing prompt diagnosis and treatment of prolonged or obstructed deliveries, is considered to be the most practical method of VVF prevention. The incidence of iatrogenic VVF is increasing globally [ 12 , 36 ]. For iatrogenic VVF, prevention during surgery is paramount, whether through careful bladder dissection or judicious use of energy devices [ 37 ]. Thus, VVF—both obstetric and iatrogenic—represents a major global problem, and many women require VVF treatment. Nevertheless, data on the clinical factors associated with successful VVF repair surgery remain limited. As outlined above, VVF repair is performed via a range of approaches, either with or without interposition flaps. Despite widespread use, the optimal approach remains uncertain and debated. Surgical repair techniques also largely depend on the skill and experience of the surgeon, and are difficult to systematically evaluate [ 1 , 38 ]. These uncertainties are clinically important because repair failure or persistent urinary incontinence can have a profound impact on women’s QoL, particularly where access to care is constrained. Existing reviews in this field are largely epidemiological or narrative in nature [ 39 ], or are restricted to iatrogenic VVF [ 21 ]. To our knowledge, no recent, methodologically robust systematic review has applied contemporary Cochrane methods—including equity‐sensitive analyses—to compare the effectiveness of surgical interventions for VVF. Additionally, at least two new randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted recently [ 40 , 41 ]. In this Cochrane review, we will synthesise the evidence on surgical treatments for both obstetric and iatrogenic VVF. We plan to perform subgroup analyses to account for the heterogeneity between these aetiologies. Objectives To assess the benefits and harms of surgical interventions for treating vesicovaginal fistula in women. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include individual RCTs and quasi‐randomised studies (i.e. studies where allocation is not necessarily random, such as by date of birth or day of the week) assessing surgery for treating vesicovaginal fistula (VVF). The intervention (VVF repair) and the critical outcome are both assessed at the individual level, rendering a cluster design unnecessary. Given the anticipated scarcity and heterogeneity of cluster‐RCTs in this field, we will exclude cluster‐RCTs and cross‐over studies. Types of participants We will include women of all ages with obstetric or iatrogenic (i.e. following a gynaecological procedure) VVF. Obstetric and iatrogenic VVF differ with respect to the background of the woman and the nature of the fistula, and we plan to perform subgroup analyses for participants with obstetric and iatrogenic VVF, as described in the Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis section. The International Continence Society (ICS) terminology divides pelvic floor fistulae broadly into childbirth‐related and non‐childbirth‐related [ 10 ], and states that caesarean section is further subclassified as an iatrogenic childbirth‐related fistula. However, in this Cochrane review we judge that, for outcomes, the key determinant is whether tissue necrosis has occurred due to obstruction; accordingly, we will examine two categories on this basis: (1) obstetric VVF due to obstructed labour; and (2) iatrogenic VVF. Obstetric VVF due to obstructed labour This category encapsulates the so‐called obstetric fistula, defined as VVF caused by obstruction or ischaemia due to delivery. Iatrogenic VVF Most cases of iatrogenic VVF occur post‐surgery, such as after total hysterectomy and caesarean section. Post‐radiotherapy VVF is also applicable. Caesarean sections due to obstructed labour (mixed obstetric and iatrogenic fistula) should only be considered in this category if intraoperative injury is obvious and clearly defined; for VVF caused predominantly by ischaemia, the definition should be obstetric VVF due to obstructed labour as mentioned above. If there is any doubt as to which is the correct classification, we will contact the study authors for further information. Eligible condition (disease identity) We include participants with VVF. Aetiologies (obstetric versus iatrogenic) are subgroups for analysis, not eligibility criteria. Ineligible conditions We will exclude participants with congenital VVF and those with other pelvic floor fistula types (e.g. uterovaginal, ureterovaginal fistulas) because the surgical procedures, prognoses, and mechanisms differ substantially from VVF and would compromise clinical homogeneity. However, as many obstetric fistulas involve the bladder neck/proximal urethra, we will include lesions that are predominantly VVF with only limited extension to these structures. We will exclude total urethro‐vaginal fistulae on the grounds of heterogeneity. Mixed populations (VVF mixed with other fistula types) If a study includes VVF together with other fistula types, we will request disaggregated data for the VVF subset. If disaggregated VVF data are available, we will include only the relevant VVF subset. If we cannot obtain such data, we will place the study in the 'Studies awaiting classification' category rather than exclude it at the eligibility stage, and we will document the reason. Mixed aetiologies within VVF (obstetric and iatrogenic not reported separately) Such trials remain eligible, and we will include them in the primary meta‐analysis as they enrol participants with the target condition (VVF). We will contact study authors to obtain stratified datasets. If unobtainable, these studies will contribute to the overall pooled estimate but will not contribute to the aetiology subgroup analyses (obstetric versus iatrogenic). Types of interventions We will include all surgical interventions for treating VVF, including the use of interposition flaps (Martius flap, gracilis muscle flaps, gluteal muscle, omentum, and peritoneum). We will consider the comparisons below. Transvaginal repair with versus without an interposition flap. Transvaginal: repair via a vaginal approach; “flap” refers to a vascularised interposition (e.g. Martius flap). Transabdominal approach with flap versus without flap. Transabdominal: repair via an abdominal approach (open, laparoscopic, or robotic); “flap” refers to a vascularised interposition (e.g. omental flap). Partial colpocleisis (e.g. Latzko procedure) versus multi‐layer closure in the transvaginal approach. Transvesical approach (e.g. O’Conor (transvesical)) versus extravesical approach in the abdominal approach. Outcome measures We will include eligible studies regardless of the outcomes reported. Critical outcomes Patient‐reported cure of or improvement in incontinence: this is assessed using the International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire‐Urinary Incontinence Short Form (ICIQ‐UI SF) [ 42 ], the Patient Global Impression of Improvement (PGI‐I) [ 43 ], or a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) [ 44 ]. This outcome includes both simple leakage due to failure of fistula closure and cases where the fistula has closed but urinary incontinence persists through the urethra (i.e. persistent urinary incontinence after fistula closure). The latter is a significant clinical issue after apparently successful closure and is frequently confused with failure of closure, i.e. extraurethral urinary incontinence. Affected women may present with stress or urgency urinary incontinence due to impaired urethral function and/or reduced bladder compliance, despite the fistula being closed. This may also be described as persistent incontinence despite fistula closure. Major adverse events: intraoperative complications: for example, blood loss, intraoperative infection, perforation or significant damage to other organs; postoperative complications: early (≤ 1 month): postoperative pain, urinary dysfunction, postoperative ileus, intra‐abdominal abscess or wound dehiscence; late (> 1 month): wound dehiscence, incisional hernia, voiding difficulty, persistent wound pain, or surgery‐related neuralgia. Studies generally use the Clavien‐Dindo classification (CDC) of surgical complications to assess the severity of adverse events [ 45 ]. We define Grade III, IV, and V as serious adverse events. In other words, these range from those that require surgical, endoscopic, or radiological intervention, to life‐threatening complications that require hospital intensive care unit management, to conditions that lead to death. If the patient has not been classified using the CDC, we will determine the severity based on whether the patient required more than the surgical treatment. Important outcomes Success rate of repair: this is defined as the anatomical closure of the fistula after treatment, which is assessed by direct visual confirmation, such as applying a dye test using methylene blue or indigo carmine, and imaging tests such as cystography. The results of repair may be divided into at least three of these categories of outcome: (1) fistula closed and woman dry; (2) fistula closed, but the woman has persistent transurethral incontinence and the reason is not ascertained; and (3) failure to close the fistula. Anatomical closure here refers to ‘fistula closed and woman dry’ and ‘fistula closed but woman has persistent transurethral incontinence and reason not ascertained’. Postoperative patient QoL, assessed by questionnaires such as the King's Health Questionnaire (KHQ) [ 46 ], and the ICIQ‐SF [ 42 ]. In particular, the KHQ is available in 39 languages and is the preferred tool because it is the most internationally versatile and was classified as grade A+ in the Fifth International Consultation on Incontinence [ 47 ]. Minor adverse events: these are defined as CDC Grades Ⅰ and Ⅱ (i.e. among the major adverse events described above). In other words, these are events that deviate from the normal postoperative course, and require pharmacological treatment or blood transfusions, but do not require surgical intervention. If CDC grading is not reported, we will classify events as minor when managed conservatively without re‐intervention and without ICU care or death. Sexual function: assessment of postoperative sexual function is important [ 48 ]. Many women with VVFs are sexually active and most want to preserve their sexual function after repair [ 49 ]. Preoperatively, women with VVF have limited sexual function due to urine leakage; however, postoperative sexual function may be limited by pain and fear. This should be assessed using questionnaires such as the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) [ 50 ]. Timing of outcome assessment After VVF repair, an initial evaluation should be performed at the time of bladder catheter removal. If the repair has not been successful, leakage will usually become evident at removal (noting that leakage may already be present before removal). Early postoperative urinary incontinence may also emerge within a few days of catheter removal [ 40 ], and that the condition often stabilises around one month postoperatively [ 51 ]. Accordingly, assessment within the first month primarily reflects early safety. In addition, there are reports of new or recurrent urinary incontinence emerging during follow‐up to approximately six months [ 33 , 52 ], indicating that reliance on the initial assessment alone may overestimate success. We therefore designate one to six months postoperatively as the primary outcome window. Many women with VVF are young, and long‐term outcomes of repair are important. Therefore, outcome assessment should also be undertaken in the long‐term (> 6 months). In summary, our time points of interest are as follows: at the time of catheter removal; < one month post‐intervention; one to six months post‐intervention; and > six months post‐intervention. If data are available at multiple points during these periods, we will use the latest time point for patient‐reported cure or improvement in incontinence, repair success rate, postoperative QoL, and sexual function. The reason for this is that the woman's healing status and recovery are naturally better reflected by long‐term outcomes. For major and minor adverse events, we will adopt the worst outcome for adverse events, as the intervention in this protocol involves surgical procedures, and the severity of complications is prioritised. Search methods for identification of studies We will not impose any language‐related or other limits during the study searches as described below. Electronic searches We will search the following electronic databases to collate all published RCTs, with no language or other limitations. We developed the search strategy for PubMed with a librarian ( Supplementary material 1 ), and conducted a pre‐search. We adopted the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy and the precision‐maximising version described in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 53 ]. Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in the Cochrane Library MEDLINE (Ovid) Embase (ProQuest Dialog) We will search all databases using recognised words (MeSH) in MEDLINE and EMTREE in Embase, and free‐text words. Searching other resources We will screen reference lists of relevant articles for potentially eligible studies. We will also search the meeting abstracts of conferences from the following sources (from 2020 to the date of search): International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) (www.figo.org); International Urogynecology Association (IUGA) (www.iuga.org); International Continence Society (ICS) (www.ics.org). To ensure the inclusion of accurate and reliable data, we will check for post‐publication amendments (retractions, expressions of concern, errata, corrigenda). We will screen PubMed linked records (Correction/Retracted Publication/Expression of Concern), Crossref/DOI status, the Retraction Watch Database ( https://retractiondatabase.org/ ), PubPeer, and Cochrane CENTRAL flags. We will re‐check these sources before final analyses and prior to publication. If an erratum/ corrigendum corrects extractable data, we will use the corrected data. If a study is retracted, we will exclude it and document the reason for exclusion. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies Two review authors (YO and TM) will independently select studies for inclusion, initially screening by title/abstract. They will assess the full‐text articles of any studies that potentially meet the inclusion criteria. In cases of disagreement, they will consult a third review author (TH). Data extraction and management Two review authors (YO and TM) will independently perform data extraction using standardised, pre‐piloted data extraction forms in Microsoft Excel. We will identify the characteristics of the studies to prepare a ‘Characteristics of included studies’ table. We will resolve any disagreements by consensus or by consulting a third review author (TH). We will extract the following data. Study information: author, year of publication, title, country (including papers published in languages other than English); funding sources and study authors’ declarations of interest. Eligibility criteria: reason for inclusion and exclusion. Study methods: trial methodology (e.g. design, randomisation sequence, stratification, allocation concealment, blinding, and recruitment details); participants: setting, number, baseline characteristics (including mean age, cause/nature of the fistula, location of the fistula, size of the fistula, number of previous attempts at repair); we will follow the genital tract fistula classification in Goh 2004 where possible [ 16 ]; interventions: surgical approach (transabdominal (laparotomy, laparoscopy, or robot‐assisted) or transvaginal) and methods (e.g. Latzko (transvaginal VVF repair), O'Conor (transabdominal VVF repair)), use of interposition flaps, interposition material, interval of intervention, and follow‐up time. Risk of bias assessment in included studies At least two review authors (YO and TM) will independently assess the risk of bias in the included studies using the revised tool to assess risk of bias in randomised trials (RoB 2) [ 54 , 55 ]. We will resolve any disagreements through discussion and, if necessary, by involving a third review author (TH). The domains of bias assessed will include the following: bias arising from the randomisation process; bias due to deviations from the intended intervention; bias due to missing outcome data; bias in measurement of the outcome; and bias in selection of the reported results. We are interested in the effect of assignment to the interventions at baseline. We will assess the outcomes and time points included in the summary of findings tables. Using the signalling questions, we will categorise each domain as either 'yes', 'probably yes', 'no', 'probably no', and 'no information'. We will classify the judgement for each domain as either 'low risk of bias', 'some concerns', or 'high risk of bias'. We will make the overall judgement about the risk of bias for the specific outcomes being assessed as follows [ 54 , 55 ]. Low risk of bias: the outcome is considered to be at low risk of bias for all domains. Some concerns: a few concerns are expected to be associated with the outcome in at least one domain but not at high risk of bias in any domain. High risk of bias: the outcome is considered to be at high risk of bias in at least one domain, or has a few concerns in multiple domains that significantly lower confidence in the result. We will summarise our findings in risk of bias tables. We will use the RoB 2 Excel tool to implement RoB 2 (available on the riskofbiasinfo.org website). Our overall risk‐of‐bias judgements will be incorporated into our GRADE assessment (see Certainty of the evidence assessment ). We will present the complete data of consensus decisions for the signalling questions in a supplemental appendix with the review. Measures of treatment effect For dichotomous outcomes, we will use risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) as the effect measures. For continuous outcomes, we will use a mean difference (MD) with 95% CIs as the effect measure for the amount of incontinence. We will also use the standardised mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs for QoL and sexual function. Where group‐specific standard deviations (SDs) are available, we will standardise by back‐transforming to a common measure. If group SDs are unavailable, we will use an external estimate of the SD from comparable studies . Unit of analysis issues In most included studies, we anticipate that the participant will be the unit of randomisation. We will analyse multi‐arm studies (i.e. studies with more than two intervention groups) using the methods outlined in Chapter 23 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 56 ]. We will prevent double‐counting of individuals by analysing each treatment arm separately against the common control group, and dividing the sample size of the common comparator group proportionately across each intervention comparison. As mentioned in the Types of studies section, we will exclude cluster‐RCTs and crossover trials from this review. Dealing with missing data We will assess studies on an intention‐to‐treat (ITT) basis as far as possible, will approach study author(s) to request information on key trial characteristics and outcome data, and will attempt to obtain missing data on the number and reasons for withdrawals and dropouts. We will report the levels of missing data as reported by the study author(s). We will assess the impact of missing data via a sensitivity analysis when we judge the RoB 2 domain ‘bias due to missing outcome data’ as at high risk. Reporting bias assessment We will report biases, such as publication bias, using funnel plots in cases where 10 or more studies are included in a meta‐analysis. We will visually assess the funnel plot for asymmetry, and will perform Egger tests to detect asymmetry [ 57 ]. Synthesis methods Our primary analysis will include all eligible studies. If sufficient studies are available for meta‐analysis, we plan to use Review Manager (RevMan) to perform a meta‐analysis using a random‐effects model for pooling data [ 58 ], since we expect clinical diversity across studies. The Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator will be used to estimate between‐trial variance (τ²). We will use the Hartung‐Knapp‐Sidik‐Jonkman method to calculate a CI for the meta‐analysis effect estimate when there are at least three included studies, and the estimate of heterogeneity is greater than zero (τ 2 > 0). In other scenarios, such as in pooled analyses of two included studies, or where the estimate of heterogeneity equals 0, we will use the Wald‐type method. If there is insufficient data for a meta‐analysis, we will use the Synthesis Without Meta‐analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline for the synthesis of intervention effects [ 59 ], if applicable, or describe narratively the results from clinically comparable trials. We will assess statistical heterogeneity by visual inspection of forest plots and describe the direction and magnitude of effects and degree of overlap between CIs. We will also use the I 2 statistic and Cochran’s test to assess statistical heterogeneity. The following guidelines will be used to interpret the I 2 statistic [ 60 ]: 0% to 40%: heterogeneity might not be important; 30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity; 75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity. Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis If a sufficient number of included studies are available to support valid subgroup comparisons, we will perform the following subgroup analyses. 1. Aetiology (obstetric VVF due to obstructed labour versus iatrogenic VVF) Obstetric and iatrogenic VVFs differ in tissue quality (ischaemia versus surgical injury) and in fistula characteristics, which may influence outcomes. We therefore prespecify a comparison of obstetric VVF (due to obstructed labour) versus iatrogenic VVF (post‐surgical, including caesarean section/hysterectomy, and post‐radiotherapy). As stated under Types of participants , we will classify caesarean sections performed for obstructed labour as iatrogenic VVF if an intraoperative injury is explicitly described; where the fistula is predominantly ischaemic, we will classify it as obstetric VVF due to obstructed labour. Where the aetiology is unclear, we will contact the study authors. For studies that report mixed populations but we are unable to separate the data for each population, we will not enter the data into the meta‐analysis, but we may describe it narratively. 2. Geographical location (LMICs versus HICs) The context in which VVF is treated likely differs across countries in terms of available personnel and medical resources, which may influence outcomes in addition to aetiology. We will pre‐specify LMICs versus HICs because the country income group may modify surgical outcomes through differences in access to experienced teams, perioperative resources, and follow‐up capacity; our a priori hypothesis is that success rates are lower in LMIC settings. For the current 2023 fiscal year, low‐income countries are defined as those with a gross national income (GNI) per capita, calculated using the World Bank Atlas method [ 61 ], of USD 1085 or less in 2021; lower middle‐income economies are those with a GNI per capita between USD 1086 and USD 4255; upper middle‐income economies are those with a GNI per capita between USD 4256 and USD 13,205; and high‐income economies are those with a GNI per capita of USD 13,205 or more. 3. Number of cases (low‐volume versus high‐volume facilities) Repair of a VVF requires a certain amount of experience, and case consolidation is also recommended due to the importance of this experience [ 62 ]. Outcomes may vary depending on the number of cases at a facility. However, there are no valid reports on the appropriate number of cases that would be sufficient experience for repair. Therefore, referring to a 2016 systematic review on the relationship between surgical volume and outcomes in gynaecological surgeries [ 63 ], we will define high‐volume facilities as those performing 12 or more VVF repair surgeries per year, and low‐volume facilities as those performing fewer than 12 per year. Although this threshold has not been specifically validated for VVF repairs, it is considered a reasonable criterion to explore potential differences in outcomes between high‐ and low‐volume centres. If the annual number of cases is not reported, we will estimate the average annual volume based on the total number of repairs performed during the study period. We will regard facilities explicitly described as “specialised fistula centres” as high‐volume centres, regardless of their reported case numbers. We will assess subgroup differences using interaction tests available within RevMan [ 58 ]. If sufficient data is unavailable to allow us to perform a subgroup analysis, we intend to describe the study narratively. Equity‐related assessment In accordance with the PROGRESS‐Plus framework [ 64 ], we will incorporate equity considerations related to geographic location. For each included study, we will extract and tabulate the World Bank country income group (LMICs versus HICs) and record the country/region for descriptive purposes. We will prespecify a single equity‐related subgroup analysis comparing LMICs versus HICs, implemented under a random‐effects model with a formal test for subgroup differences. If the number of studies is insufficient for a formal subgroup analysis, we will summarise the LMICs versus HICs findings descriptively. We will briefly note any reported contextual determinants relevant to equity (e.g. access constraints) and discuss implications for health equity and access in the Discussion section, along with the rationale for focusing on LMICs versus HICs. Sensitivity analysis We will assess the impact of sensitivity analyses on the overall estimates of treatment effects and on measures of heterogeneity. If we observe meaningful changes, we will explore specific reasons for these changes and discuss how they affect the overall conclusions. To assess the influence of studies with a high overall risk of bias, we will repeat the analyses for the critical outcomes after excluding studies judged at overall high risk of bias for the outcome (RoB 2). Certainty of the evidence assessment We will use the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence and present outcome data in summary of findings tables [ 65 ]. We will use the five GRADE domains (study limitations, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias) to assess the certainty of the body of evidence. Our overall risk of bias assessments using the RoB 2 tool will feed directly into the assessment of study limitations. We will justify all decisions to downgrade the certainty of evidence using footnotes. We will prepare summary of findings tables using the GRADEpro software [ 66 ]. Two review authors (TM and YO) will independently assess the certainty of the evidence, and will resolve any disagreements either through discussion or by involving a third review author (TH). We will justify our judgements, and document and incorporate them into our reporting of results. We have selected the following comparisons because we believe these to be the most relevant and important comparisons. Transvaginal repair with versus without an interposition flap Transabdominal approach with flap versus without flap Partial colpocleisis (e.g. Latzko procedure) versus multi‐layer closure in transvaginal approach Transvesical approach (e.g. O’Conor (transvesical)) versus extravesical approach in abdominal approach For the four comparisons, we plan to present the following critical and important outcomes in the summary of findings tables. Patient‐reported cure or improvement in incontinence (1 to 6 months post‐intervention): there are a substantial number of failures between 1 month and 6 months post‐operatively. Therefore, for the summary of findings tables, we will use the latest available assessment time point within 1 to 6 months post‐intervention (i.e. the longest follow‐up within this window). Major adverse events: these most commonly occur within the first month. However, severity rather than timing is paramount, so we will use the worst (most severe) event recorded, irrespective of the assessment time point. Success rate of repair (1 to 6 months post‐intervention). For the same reason as mentioned in 'Patient‐reported cure or improvement in incontinence' above, we will set this period accordingly. Postoperative patient QoL (> 6 months post‐intervention). QoL reflects a woman's QoL more accurately over longer periods. However, from the practical perspective of consolidating available studies, we will set the primary measurement point as six months postoperatively. Consumer involvement We do not plan to involve consumers in this review. This is due to limited resources and anticipated difficulties identifying and supporting contributors with lived experience of VVF across settings. documents.title: Transvaginal mesh or grafts or native tissue repair for vaginal prolapse.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelvic organ prolapse is the descent of one or more of the pelvic organs (uterus, vaginal apex, bladder, or bowel) into the vagina. In recent years, surgeons have increasingly used grafts in transvaginal repairs. Graft material can be synthetic or biological. The aim is to reduce prolapse recurrence and surpass the effectiveness of traditional native tissue repair (colporrhaphy) for vaginal prolapse. This is a review update; the previous version was published in 2016.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the safety and effectiveness of transvaginal mesh or biological grafts compared to native tissue repair or other grafts in the surgical treatment of vaginal prolapse.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register, which contains trials identified from the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and two clinical trials registers (March 2022).
SELECTION CRITERIA: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different types of vaginal repair (mesh, biological graft, or native tissue).
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors independently selected trials, assessed risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcomes were awareness of prolapse, repeat surgery, and recurrent prolapse on examination.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 51 RCTs (7846 women). The certainty of the evidence was largely moderate (ranging from very low to moderate). Transvaginal permanent mesh versus native tissue repair Awareness of prolapse at six months to seven years was less likely after mesh repair (risk ratio (RR) 0.83, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.73 to 0.95; I2 = 34%; 17 studies, 2932 women; moderate-certainty evidence). This suggests that if 23% of women are aware of prolapse after native tissue repair, between 17% and 22% will be aware of prolapse after permanent mesh repair. Rates of repeat surgery for prolapse were lower in the mesh group (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.95; I2 = 35%; 17 studies, 2485 women; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference between the groups in rates of repeat surgery for incontinence (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.59; I2 = 0%; 13 studies, 2206 women; moderate-certainty evidence). However, more women in the mesh group required repeat surgery for the combined outcome of prolapse, stress incontinence, or mesh exposure (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.26; I2 = 54%; 27 studies, 3916 women; low-certainty evidence). This suggests that if 7.1% of women require repeat surgery after native tissue repair, between 7.6% and 16% will require repeat surgery after permanent mesh repair. The rate of mesh exposure was 11.8% and surgery for mesh exposure was 6.1% in women who had mesh repairs. Recurrent prolapse on examination was less likely after mesh repair (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.55; I2 = 84%; 25 studies, 3680 women; very low-certainty evidence). Permanent transvaginal mesh was associated with higher rates of de novo stress incontinence (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.88; I2 = 0%; 17 studies, 2001 women; moderate-certainty evidence) and bladder injury (RR 3.67, 95% CI 1.63 to 8.28; I2 = 0%; 14 studies, 1997 women; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference between the groups in rates of de novo dyspareunia (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.79; I2 = 27%; 16 studies, 1308 women; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference in quality of life outcomes; however, there was substantial heterogeneity in the data. Transvaginal absorbable mesh versus native tissue repair There was no evidence of a difference between the two methods of repair at two years for the rate of awareness of prolapse (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.44; 1 study, 54 women), rate of repeat surgery for prolapse (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.09 to 2.40; 1 study, 66 women), or recurrent prolapse on examination (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.70; 1 study, 66 women). The effect of either form of repair was uncertain for bladder-related outcomes, dyspareunia, and quality of life. Transvaginal biological graft versus native tissue repair There was no evidence of a difference between the groups at one to three years for the outcome awareness of prolapse (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.56; I2 = 0%; 8 studies, 1374 women; moderate-certainty evidence), repeat surgery for prolapse (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.77; I2 = 0%; 6 studies, 899 women; moderate-certainty evidence), and recurrent prolapse on examination (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.29; I2 = 53%; 9 studies, 1278 women; low-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference between the groups for dyspareunia or quality of life. Transvaginal permanent mesh versus any other permanent mesh or biological graft vaginal repair Sparse reporting of primary outcomes in both comparisons significantly limited any meaningful analysis.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: While transvaginal permanent mesh is associated with lower rates of awareness of prolapse, repeat surgery for prolapse, and prolapse on examination than native tissue repair, it is also associated with higher rates of total repeat surgery (for prolapse, stress urinary incontinence, or mesh exposure), bladder injury, and de novo stress urinary incontinence. While the direction of effects and effect sizes are relatively unchanged from the 2016 version of this review, the certainty and precision of the findings have all improved with a larger sample size. In addition, the clinical relevance of these data has improved, with 10 trials reporting 3- to 10-year outcomes. The risk-benefit profile means that transvaginal mesh has limited utility in primary surgery. Data on the management of recurrent prolapse are of limited quality. Given the risk-benefit profile, we recommend that any use of permanent transvaginal mesh should be conducted under the oversight of the local ethics committee in compliance with local regulatory recommendations. Data are not supportive of absorbable meshes or biological grafts for the management of transvaginal prolapse.

documents.title: Long-term outcomes of surgical interventions for stress urinary incontinence: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stress urinary incontinence is common among women, and surgical interventions have significantly improved patients' symptoms. The long-term effectiveness of these surgeries is increasingly drawing attention, yet it remains sparsely documented in the literature.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the long-term effectiveness and safety of retropubic tension-free vaginal tape (TVT-RP), tension-free vaginal tape-obturator (TVT-O), transobturator tape (TOT), single-incision sling (SIS), Burch colposuspension, and pubovaginal sling (PVS).
METHODS: A comprehensive and systematic literature review was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, Medicine, and clinicaltrials.gov from inception to May 2023. Selected trials were evaluated for potential bias using the Cochrane tool. Treatment modalities were compared using network meta-analysis to assess objective success rate, subjective success rate, and complications as outcomes.
RESULTS: A total of 37 studies involving 5720 patients were included. No significant statistical differences were found among the interventions regarding objective success rate. PVS had the highest surface under the cumulative ranking curve SUCRA value (93.1). For subjective success rate, TVT-RP, TVT-O, and PVS demonstrated superiority over SIS, with PVS having the highest SUCRA value (80.1). SIS had lower overall complication and pain rates compared to other methods, with statistical significance. There were no differences in reoperation rate, exposure rate, and urinary tract infection occurrence among the surgical approaches.
CONCLUSIONS: In terms of long-term effectiveness and safety, TVT-RP and TVT-O appear to be the preferred options for patients opting for synthetic slings, while for patients seeking nonsynthetic slings, PVS may represent the optimal choice.
documents.conclusions: In terms of long-term effectiveness and safety, TVT-RP and TVT-O appear to be the preferred options for patients opting for synthetic slings, while for patients seeking nonsynthetic slings, PVS may represent the optimal choice.
